title: The Copper Country to the Castle Church: the Miner's Son, the Vow at Stotternheim, and the Door
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Eisleben, the birth in the mining town
stops.date_confidence: attested; the year is calculated back from the baptism, and Luther himself was never certain whether he was born in 1483 or 1484
stops.campa: Hans Luder, a peasant's son who has left the land for the copper trade, and his wife Margarethe are lodging in Eisleben in the county of Mansfeld when their son is born in the night. The town lives on the copper shale beneath it: shafts, smelters, the smell of roasted ore in the streets. The father is not yet a master, only a miner working another man's pit. The child takes the family name in its Saxon form, Luder, and will spell it Luther only as a grown man, once he has begun signing letters that the whole of Germany reads.
suggested_refs: Luthers Geburtshaus, Eisleben, rebuilt after the fire of 1689 and museumized from 1693
sources: Martin Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation 1483-1521

stops.name: Eisleben, the font on Saint Martin's day
stops.date_confidence: attested by Eisleben parish tradition; no baptismal register survives from that year
stops.campa: The child is carried the short distance to the parish church of St. Peter and Paul the morning after his birth and baptized in its font. The day is the eleventh of November, feast of St. Martin of Tours, the soldier who cut his cloak in half at the gate of Amiens, and the boy is named for him. Nothing else about the ceremony is recorded. The font is later removed from the church and returned to it in the twentieth century. It stands there now, the one object that certainly touched him on his second day of life.
suggested_refs: The late-Gothic bronze font of St. Petri-Pauli, Eisleben

stops.name: Mansfeld, the smelter's house
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted, the move is dated only to Luther's first year
stops.campa: Within the first year the family moves the few miles to Mansfeld, where Hans leases smelting furnaces and rises from wage miner to Huettenmeister, master of the works, eventually sitting among the town's four elected representatives. The house on the slope below the counts' castle is built of stone, not timber. Martin is sent to the town Latin school and learns grammar under the rod; he remembers, fifty years later, being beaten fifteen times in a single morning. The father intends a lawyer, says so plainly, and pays for it.
suggested_refs: Luthers Elternhaus, Mansfeld, excavated 2003 and opened as a museum in 2014
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation
Luther's Table Talk (reported speech, for the schoolroom detail)

stops.name: Magdeburg, the year among the Brethren
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At thirteen he is sent north to Magdeburg for a year of schooling among the Brethren of the Common Life, the devotio moderna men who teach copying, plain piety, and the interior life. He and his fellows sing for bread in the streets, a practice the schools sanction and the boys endure. In Magdeburg he sees a prince of Anhalt who has given away everything going through the town as a mendicant friar, so wasted by fasting that he looks like a death's head, and the townspeople bowing as he passes. The picture stays with him for fifty years.
suggested_refs: The Magdeburg house of the Brethren of the Common Life, dissolved in the Reformation

stops.name: Eisenach, the chorister at the Cotta table
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He goes on to Eisenach, where his mother's people live, and boards with the family of Ursula Cotta while attending the school at St. George's. He sings again for alms as a chorister, and this time the singing brings him a table rather than a doorstep. Here he gets the Latin that will let him read anything, a firmer classical grounding than Mansfeld gave, along with the friendship of the vicar Johannes Braun. The Wartburg stands over the town on its rock. He will come back to it under another name, hunted, twenty-three years later.
suggested_refs: The Lutherhaus at Eisenach, the timber house associated with the Cotta family

segments.name: Erfurt: the Law, the Storm, the Cloister

stops.name: Erfurt, matriculation at the Collegium Maius
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At seventeen he matriculates at Erfurt, the largest university in the German lands, entered in the register as Martinus Ludher ex Mansfelt and able to pay his own fees, which not every student can. He takes the baccalaureate in 1502 and the master of arts in the spring of 1505, second of seventeen candidates, walking in the procession with a torch. His father buys him a Corpus Juris and addresses him from that day in the formal Ihr rather than the familiar du. In May he enters the faculty of law. He lasts in it six weeks.
suggested_refs: The Collegium Maius of the University of Erfurt, destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt in 1999
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Stotternheim, the road in the storm
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the whole episode rests on Luther's own recollection told decades later at table, and on nothing written in 1505
stops.campa: Returning to Erfurt from a visit home, he is overtaken on the road by a thunderstorm and thrown to the ground by a bolt that strikes close beside him. He cries out to the patron of the mining country: Help me, Saint Anne, I will become a monk. No document from that summer mentions it; the account is his own, given long afterward. A stone marks the traditional place between Stotternheim and the city. What is documented is the consequence. Fifteen days later he sells his law books, keeps Virgil and Plautus, and gives a farewell supper.
suggested_refs: The Lutherstein between Stotternheim and Erfurt, erected 1917
sources: Wikipedia, 'Martin Luther' (traditional account, tagged as such)

stops.name: Erfurt, the gate of the Augustinians
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He knocks at the gate of the Observant Augustinians, the strictest house in Erfurt, and is admitted. His friends walk him to the door in tears; his father, when the news reaches Mansfeld, is furious and says the vow may well have come from the devil. Inside, the novice sweeps the floors, begs through the town with a sack, and confesses for hours at a stretch, sometimes six hours over a single day's sins, until Johann von Staupitz tells him to come back with a sin worth absolving. He is looking for a gracious God in the cloister and cannot find one there.
suggested_refs: The Augustinerkloster at Erfurt, with the cell traditionally shown as Luther's
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Erfurt Cathedral, the hands laid on
stops.date_confidence: attested, but the day is split between sources: German Wikipedia gives 4 April 1507, English Wikipedia gives 3-4 April; not adjudicated here
stops.campa: In the cathedral above the market steps the auxiliary bishop Johann Bonemilch von Laasphe lays hands on him and he is made a priest. He is twenty-three. The power now placed in his hands, to hold God in bread, frightens him more than it consoles him; he says later that at the altar he was so stupefied he could barely get through the canon. The vow sworn on the Stotternheim road binds in this building, twenty-one months after the storm. From this day he may say Mass, and he says his first one a month later in his own house.
suggested_refs: The Erfurter Dom (Mariendom), seat of the ordination

stops.name: Erfurt, the first Mass and the father's answer
stops.date_confidence: attested; the research pool had merged this with the ordination a month earlier, and the two are separated here
stops.campa: A month after ordination he sings his first Mass in the monastery church, and Hans Luder rides over from Mansfeld with twenty horsemen and a gift of twenty gulden, still angry. At the feast afterward the son asks the father across the table why he opposed the cloister, and cites the thunderclap. The father answers in front of the guests: have you not read that you should honour your father and your mother? Nobody laughs. The words lodge, and Luther quotes them back at himself sixteen years later when he writes against monastic vows.
suggested_refs: The Augustinian monastery church at Erfurt, site of the Primiz of 2 May 1507
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Wittenberg, a year of Aristotle at the Leucorea
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Staupitz sends him to the Elector Frederick's new university at Wittenberg, six years old and built on sand at the edge of the Saxon plain, to lecture on the Nicomachean Ethics. He dislikes the assignment and calls the town the border of civilisation. It lasts one year; then Erfurt recalls him. Eight decades later Giordano Bruno teaches two free years in this same faculty. He calls it Luther's own university and the cradle of the whole business, and leaves with an oration praising the courage of the man who is here now, grumbling about Aristotle.
suggested_refs: The Leucorea, University of Wittenberg, founded 1502 by Frederick the Wise
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Rome, the precinct of the old basilica
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stay of about four weeks in the winter of 1510-1511; the exact month is not fixed
stops.campa: Sent south on business of the order, in a quarrel over the union of the Observant and Conventual houses, he walks to Rome with a companion and stays about a month. He makes the pilgrim rounds, says Masses at the holy places, and finds the Roman clergy careless: priests racing through the liturgy at speed, jokes made at the altar, six Masses said in the time he needs for one. The old basilica of St. Peter is coming down around him and the new one is going up on indulgence money. He does not yet know that this is what he is looking at.
stops.quote: Why does not the pope, whose wealth is to-day greater than the riches of the richest, build just this one church of St. Peter with his own money, rather than with the money of poor believers?
stops.quote_source: Ninety-Five Theses, Thesis 86, Project Gutenberg #274 (written 1517, seven years after the visit)
suggested_refs: Old St. Peter's Basilica in demolition, 1510, and Bramante's rising replacement
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation
Project Gutenberg #274, Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences

stops.name: Rome, the holy stairs by the Lateran
stops.date_confidence: tradition, resting on Luther's own table talk and a later note by his son Paul; no contemporary record, and month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: The tradition has him climb the holy stairs on his knees, a Pater Noster on each step, to free his grandfather's soul from purgatory, and at the top, straightening up, wonder aloud whether any of it is true. Nothing written in 1511 confirms the climb. What is certain is that he goes to Rome believing the machinery works and comes home describing the city as a market where anything can be bought, souls included. The doubt is dated to these stairs only by hindsight, and the hindsight is his own.
suggested_refs: The Scala Sancta at the Lateran, marble stairs cased in wood since 1723
sources: Bainton, Here I Stand, noting the story rests on later Table Talk recollection rather than a contemporary record

stops.name: Wittenberg, the transfer to the Black Cloister
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1511; day defaulted
stops.campa: Staupitz transfers him permanently from Erfurt to Wittenberg in the autumn, over the objection of the Erfurt house, which holds the grudge for years and will refuse him its goodwill at the worst moment. He moves into the Augustinian cloister at the eastern end of the town, a long unfinished building of black-robed friars from which the name Schwarzes Kloster comes. He will live in it for thirty-five years: first as a monk under vows, then as an outlaw of the Empire, then as a married man with six children, boarders, and students taking notes at his table.
suggested_refs: The Schwarzes Kloster, Wittenberg, later the Lutherhaus
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Wittenberg, the doctor's ring and the chair
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Staupitz, who wants his own teaching load lifted, makes him take the doctorate over his protest that he is too weak and will not live long. He swears the doctor's oath to expound scripture faithfully, receives the ring and the cap, and succeeds his confessor in the chair of biblical theology. He holds that chair until he dies, and he will appeal to that oath every time he is asked by what authority a friar contradicts Rome. Two hundred and eighty-two years later Novalis, schooled at Eisleben where this man was born, takes his law degree from this university.
suggested_refs: The doctoral oath of the Wittenberg theological faculty, sworn 19 October 1512
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Wittenberg, the Castle Church and the ninety-five propositions
stops.date_confidence: attested for the letter to Albert of Mainz; the door-posting on the same day is disputed, Melanchthon and Roerer against Luther's own 1517 silence, and Iserloh 1961 against both
stops.campa: On the eve of All Saints, when the Elector's relic collection will be shown and indulgences attached to the viewing of it, he writes to Albert of Mainz protesting the traffic in pardons and encloses ninety-five propositions for academic debate. Whether he also nails a copy to the door of the Castle Church that day is not agreed: Melanchthon says so after Luther is dead, Georg Roerer notes it in a margin, and Luther's own letters of 1517 mention only the archbishop. The door is the university's notice board. The debate he proposes never takes place.
stops.quote: Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, when He said Poenitentiam agite, willed that the whole life of believers should be repentance.
suggested_refs: The north door of the Schlosskirche, Wittenberg, burned 1760 and replaced in bronze 1858
sources: Erwin Iserloh (1961), summarized in the historiographical debate

stops.name: Heidelberg, the theology of the cross
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Augustinians of the German congregation hold their chapter at Heidelberg and, instead of silencing him, invite him to preside at a disputation. He argues a theology of the cross against a theology of glory: that God is found where he is hidden, in suffering and shame, and not in works anyone can see. The older men are unmoved. The younger ones are not. Martin Bucer, a Dominican at the time, writes an excited letter about what he has heard; Johannes Brenz and Erhard Schnepf are in the room. The southern German reformation starts in that hall.
stops.quote: Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt, even without letters of pardon.
suggested_refs: The forty theological and philosophical theses of the Heidelberg Disputation
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Augsburg, three days before Cajetan
stops.date_confidence: attested to 12-14 October 1518
stops.campa: Summoned to Augsburg during the imperial diet, he lodges with the Carmelites at St. Anna and is examined over three days by Cardinal Cajetan, the ablest Thomist in Europe, at the Fugger townhouse on the Maximilianstrasse where the cardinal is staying. Cajetan wants one word, revoco, I recant. Luther asks to be shown from scripture where he errs. On the third day the cardinal loses his temper and orders him out of his sight. Warned that an order for his arrest may exist, he leaves the city at night through a small gate, on horseback, without trousers.
stops.quote: They preach man who say that so soon as the penny jingles into the money-box, the soul flies out [of purgatory].
stops.quote_source: Ninety-Five Theses, Thesis 27, Project Gutenberg #274; the bracketed words are the translator's completion
suggested_refs: St. Anna, Augsburg, the Carmelite house that lodged him, later the first Lutheran church in the city

stops.name: Leipzig, the Pleissenburg and the name of Hus
stops.date_confidence: attested; the disputation ran 27 June to 16 July 1519, with Luther facing Eck from 4 July
stops.campa: In the great hall of the Pleissenburg, under Duke George's guard, Johann Eck debates Karlstadt for a fortnight and then Luther for a week. Eck works him steadily toward the ground he wants. If popes and councils can err, what was the Council of Constance doing when it burned Jan Hus? Luther answers that among the articles condemned at Constance there were some plainly Christian and evangelical. The hall stirs. Duke George is heard to swear from his seat. Luther has said in public that a general council burned a man for telling the truth.
stops.quote: The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and the grace of God.
suggested_refs: The Pleissenburg at Leipzig, demolished 1897; the New Town Hall stands on the site
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Wittenberg, the bull burned at the Elster Gate
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Sixty days after Exsurge Domine reaches him with its threat of excommunication, he walks out of the eastern gate with the university following. A fire is lit on the knacker's field beyond the wall. Volumes of canon law go in first, then the decretals, then the bull itself, which he holds up and drops with a formula of his own: because you have troubled the Holy One of the Lord, may everlasting fire trouble you. The students sing a Te Deum and spend the afternoon carting mock bulls around town on a wagon. An oak stands on the spot now, itself a replacement.
stops.quote: They will be condemned eternally, together with their teachers, who believe themselves sure of their salvation because they have letters of pardon.
suggested_refs: The Luthereiche at Wittenberg, marking the burning of the bull, replanted more than once

stops.name: Worms, the table of books
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He enters the city on the sixteenth with two thousand people in the streets to see him, and is brought the next afternoon to the bishop's palace beside the cathedral, where Charles V sits with the electors. The emperor is twenty-one and holds Spain, the Netherlands, Austria, and the Indies. Some twenty of Luther's books lie stacked on a bench. Asked whether they are his and whether he will retract them, he answers in a voice so low that men at the back complain they cannot hear him, and asks for a day. Worms has held such assemblies since Charlemagne judged the Saxon war here.
stops.quote: The ravens must have a kite.
stops.quote_source: Table Talk, Project Gutenberg #9841, trans. Captain Henry Bell, section 'The World must have stern and fierce Rulers'; Luther's reply when told Charles had been elected Emperor. Reported speech recorded by dinner guests, not autograph
suggested_refs: The Bischofshof at Worms, demolished in the eighteenth century; the site is marked in the cathedral garden

stops.name: Worms, the refusal by torchlight
stops.date_confidence: attested; the closing words are only partly documented, see quote_source
stops.campa: Brought back at six in the evening, in a hall so crowded that torches have to be lit, he divides his books into three kinds and refuses to disown any of them. Pressed for a plain answer without horns or teeth, he says that unless he is convicted by scripture or by evident reason his conscience is captive to the word of God, and that to act against conscience is neither safe nor honest. Then the ending. In these same weeks, under this same emperor, Hernan Cortes is closing his siege lines around Tenochtitlan. Charles is trying two revolts at once, on two hemispheres.
stops.quote_source: The documented close of Luther's reply at Worms, 18 April 1521. The famous continuation 'Hier stehe ich, ich kann nicht anders' is traditional and absent from the primary record; Wikipedia flags it 'according to tradition'
suggested_refs: The Reichstag hall of the Bischofshof at Worms, 18 April 1521
sources: Wikipedia, 'Here I stand, I can do no other'

stops.name: Worms, the Edict against a man already gone
stops.date_confidence: attested; the document is backdated to 8 May
stops.campa: With most of the estates gone home, Charles has the edict drawn and signs it: Luther is an outlaw, no one may shelter or feed him, his books are to be burned everywhere, and any man may kill him without penalty. It is backdated to the eighth of May to make it look like the act of a full diet. The city where this is signed is the one where Bernard of Clairvaux came down the Rhine in 1146 to stop a monk preaching massacre against the Jews of Worms and Mainz, and where the Heiliger Sand, the oldest surviving Jewish cemetery in Europe, holds the grandfather of Felix Adler.
suggested_refs: The Edict of Worms, signed 25 May 1521, never fully enforced in Saxony

stops.name: Wartburg Castle, the abduction and the eleven weeks
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Riding home through the Thuringian forest near Altenstein he is taken by armed men, pulled from the wagon, and carried by a roundabout road up to the Wartburg above Eisenach, the castle he could see from the schoolroom as a boy. Frederick the Wise has arranged the ambush and arranges not to be told where the prisoner is kept, so that he can swear he does not know. Luther grows a beard, wears a knight's clothes, calls himself Junker Joerg, and turns the Greek New Testament into German in eleven weeks. In 1817 Ludwig Jahn's students climb this rock on the theses' tercentenary and burn books of their own.
stops.quote: We do not have to ask about the literal Latin or how we are to speak German, as these asses do. Rather we must ask the mother in the home, the children on the street, the common person in the market about this.
stops.quote_source: An Open Letter on Translating (Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen), Project Gutenberg #272, written 1530 in defence of the translation begun here
suggested_refs: The Lutherstube at the Wartburg, the study of the translation
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Wartburg Castle, the inkwell and the wall
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated; no source from 1521 or 1522 records it, and the date here is a placeholder within the Wartburg months
stops.campa: The story is that the devil came into the study to interrupt the translation, and that Luther threw the inkwell at him, and that the stain stayed on the plaster. Nothing written during the Wartburg months mentions it. The mark shown to visitors has been renewed again and again, because for three centuries tourists scratched at the wall and carried the plaster home in their pockets. What the room actually holds is a table, a window over the forest, a whale vertebra used as a footstool, and the place where one man alone with a Greek text decided how German would be written.
suggested_refs: The ink stain of the Lutherstube, repeatedly restored through the nineteenth century
sources: nineteenth-century travel accounts noting the stain's repeated restoration

stops.name: Jena, the Black Bear and the two Swiss
stops.date_confidence: attested by Kessler's account, written down years later
stops.campa: On the road back to Wittenberg, still in disguise, he stops at the Black Bear in Jena and takes a table with a Hebrew psalter open in front of him. Two Swiss students walking to Wittenberg sit down with him. He asks them what people are saying about Luther in Switzerland, tells them the man will be found at Wittenberg, pays for their meal, and lets them go on calling him sir knight. Johannes Kessler works out afterward who bought his dinner and writes the scene down years later in his Sabbata, which is why one evening of this life is recorded by strangers.
suggested_refs: The Gasthof Zum Schwarzen Baeren at Jena, still standing on the Lutherplatz
sources: Johannes Kessler, Sabbata, cited in Bainton, Here I Stand

stops.name: Wittenberg, eight sermons in Invocavit week
stops.date_confidence: attested; the eight sermons run 9 to 16 March 1522
stops.campa: Karlstadt and the Zwickau prophets have been pulling down images, smashing altars, and abolishing the Mass while he was hidden. He comes back without the Elector's leave, still under the ban, and preaches eight days running from the town church pulpit, one sermon a day through Invocavit week. The argument is that faith cannot be compelled and that a conscience not yet taught must not be dragged along: he opposed indulgences, he says, but never used force, and the word did everything while he sat still and drank Wittenberg beer. The images stay up. Karlstadt leaves town.
suggested_refs: The Invokavitpredigten of March 1522, preached in the Stadtkirche St. Marien
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: His Road to Reformation

stops.name: Wittenberg, the September Testament off the press
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1522; day defaulted
stops.campa: Melchior Lotter's press prints the German New Testament in an edition of about three thousand, without the translator's name on it, with twenty-one woodcuts from the Cranach workshop for Revelation in which the whore of Babylon wears a papal tiara. It sells out in three months at the price of half a week's wages for a journeyman. Duke George bans it in ducal Saxony and orders copies bought up at his own cost; his subjects buy them faster than his agents do. Luther keeps revising the text for the remaining twenty-four years of his life and never lets it stand.
stops.quote: Faith, as the chief work, and no other work, has given us the name of 'believers on Christ.'
stops.quote_source: A Treatise on Good Works, Project Gutenberg #418, 1520
suggested_refs: The September Testament of 1522, printed by Melchior Lotter the Younger

stops.name: Nimbschen, the wagon and the herring barrels
stops.date_confidence: attested; the escape falls on the night before Easter 1523
stops.campa: Twelve nuns of the Cistercian house at Nimbschen, in ducal Saxony where helping a nun escape is a capital matter, write to Luther for help. On the night before Easter the Torgau merchant Leonhard Koppe drives his covered wagon out of the convent yard with them hidden in it among the herring barrels he has just delivered. Three go home to their families. Nine arrive in Wittenberg with nothing at all. One of them, twenty-four years old and of the poorer Saxon nobility, is called Katharina von Bora, and she refuses the first two husbands proposed for her.
suggested_refs: Kloster Nimbschen near Grimma, dissolved 1536, now a ruin
sources: Coordinate approximate: Kloster Nimbschen south of Grimma on the Mulde, not verified in the geography pass

stops.name: Frankenhausen, the wagon fort broken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The peasant bands of Thuringia, some eight thousand of them, stand on a hill outside Frankenhausen behind a ring of wagons while Thomas Muentzer preaches that God will catch the cannonballs in his sleeves. The princes' artillery opens. The rout kills perhaps six thousand in an afternoon; Muentzer is found hiding in a bed in the town and beheaded ten days later. Luther has already published Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants, telling the lords to stab, smite, and slay. He never withdraws it. The peasants who had been reading him stop reading him.
suggested_refs: The Schlachtberg above Bad Frankenhausen and Werner Tuebke's panorama painting of the battle
sources: Coordinate is the town of Bad Frankenhausen, not the battlefield hill above it; not verified in the geography pass

stops.name: Wittenberg, the monk marries the nun
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries Katharina von Bora in the cloister on a Tuesday evening, in haste and nearly in secret, with Bugenhagen officiating and Justus Jonas, the jurist Johann Apel, and Lucas and Barbara Cranach standing as witnesses. He is forty-one, she twenty-six, both of them under vows they have renounced. He says he did it to please his father, to spite the pope and the devil, and because the world is ending anyway. Erasmus writes that the reformation is a comedy ending in a wedding. The cloister the Elector gives them has forty rooms and almost no furniture.
stops.quote: A Christian man is the most free lord of all, and subject to none; a Christian man is the most dutiful servant of all, and subject to every one.
stops.quote_source: Concerning Christian Liberty, opening propositions, Project Gutenberg #1911, 1520
suggested_refs: The Lutherhaus at Wittenberg, wedding place and household for the next twenty-one years

stops.name: Wittenberg, the wedding walked through the street
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Two weeks later the public celebration is held: a procession to the town church for the blessing, a feast in the cloister afterward, guests riding in from Mansfeld including his parents, twenty gulden from the town council and a barrel of Einbeck beer from the Elector. Wittenberg turns out to look at the monk and the nun. Bugenhagen gives the blessing before the whole town. The bells are rung and the mayor walks in the procession. It is done in the street, in daylight.
suggested_refs: The Stadtkirche St. Marien, Wittenberg, where Bugenhagen gave the public blessing

stops.name: Wittenberg, the answer to Erasmus
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1525; day defaulted
stops.campa: Erasmus, pushed for a year by Rome and by Henry VIII to break with him, published On Free Will in the autumn of 1524. Luther takes fourteen months and answers with De Servo Arbitrio, the one book of his own he later says is worth keeping along with the catechism. The will, he argues, is a beast ridden either by God or by Satan, and it does not choose its rider. Erasmus never forgives it. Seven years later, hearing of Giulio Camillo's memory theatre, he writes that the thing could raise a tragedy in the schools of Italy as great as Luther's in religion.
stops.quote: If our sins could be removed by our own efforts, what need was there for the Son of God to be given for them?
stops.quote_source: Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, Project Gutenberg #1549, 1535
suggested_refs: De Servo Arbitrio (On the Bondage of the Will), Wittenberg, December 1525

stops.name: Marburg Castle, the chalk under the cloth
stops.date_confidence: attested; the colloquy runs 1 to 4 October 1529
stops.campa: Philip of Hesse brings the Wittenbergers and the Swiss up to his castle above Marburg to make one Protestant front against the emperor. They agree on fourteen articles and most of a fifteenth. On the supper they do not agree. Luther chalks Hoc est corpus meum on the table before the talking starts, covers it with a velvet cloth, and will not be moved off the words. Zwingli says the body is in heaven and the bread is a sign of it. Luther refuses him the hand of brotherhood. Paracelsus is that same decade scandalising Basel down the Rhine, in Erasmus and Froben's circle.
suggested_refs: The Marburg Articles of October 1529, agreed on fourteen points and divided on the fifteenth

segments.name: The Fortress and the Late Work

stops.name: Coburg, the diet attended by letter
stops.date_confidence: attested; Luther is at the Veste Coburg from 23 April to 4 October 1530
stops.campa: Under the imperial ban he cannot go to Augsburg, so he sits out the diet from April to October in the fortress above Coburg, the southernmost point of Saxon soil, writing several letters a day to Melanchthon, who is losing his nerve by the hour. The confession is read aloud to Charles V on the twenty-fifth of June by the Saxon chancellor Christian Beyer, in German, loudly enough to carry into the courtyard. Melanchthon wrote it and does not read it. Three hundred years later Hegel, rector at Berlin, gives the tercentenary address on that document.
suggested_refs: The Lutherstube at the Veste Coburg, where he waited out the Diet of Augsburg
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: The Preservation of the Church

stops.name: Wittenberg, the whole Bible in one folio
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Hans Lufft prints the complete Bible at Wittenberg: Old Testament, Apocrypha, New Testament, seventy-five books in six parts with a hundred and seventeen woodcuts, a folio costing about two and a half gulden unbound. The Old Testament has taken twelve years and a committee, Melanchthon on the Greek, Aurogallus on the Hebrew, a butcher brought in to name the parts of a sheep for Leviticus and the court jeweller consulted on the stones in Revelation. Lufft prints a hundred thousand copies over forty years. The German everyone writes afterward is this book's German.
stops.quote: I am persuaded, said he, that it costeth God yearly more to maintain only the sparrows than the yearly revenue of the French King amounteth unto.
stops.quote_source: Table Talk, Project Gutenberg #9841, trans. Captain Henry Bell. Reported speech recorded by dinner guests, not autograph; the speech tag is in the printed text
suggested_refs: The 1534 Wittenberg Bible printed by Hans Lufft, with hand-coloured woodcuts from the Cranach workshop

stops.name: Schmalkalden, the testament set aside
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1537 for the assembly; day defaulted. The articles themselves were written at Wittenberg in December 1536, not here
stops.campa: The Elector has him draw up articles in December, at Wittenberg, stating what can and cannot be conceded to a papal council. He writes them expecting to die and calls them his testament. At Schmalkalden in February the kidney stone stops him completely; he is carried out of the town half dead in a wagon, passes the stone on the road, and recovers. The League does not adopt his articles. It takes Melanchthon's treatise on the pope's power instead, while the man himself lies in a wagon outside the town.
stops.quote: I would rather expose myself to endure all the torments that this world, flesh, and the devil were able to devise and prepare than to give my consent thereunto.
stops.quote_source: Table Talk, Project Gutenberg #9841, trans. Captain Henry Bell, section on judging causes of religion by God's word rather than human wisdom. Reported speech
suggested_refs: The Smalcald Articles, written at Wittenberg December 1536, adopted only later as a Lutheran confessional document
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: The Preservation of the Church

stops.name: Torgau, the chapel built for preaching
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He rides to Torgau to consecrate the chapel the Elector John Frederick has built inside Hartenfels Castle, a room designed from the first stone for Protestant worship: the pulpit set in the middle of the long wall, no screen between clergy and people, galleries so that everyone can hear a voice. He preaches that nothing should happen in it except that God speak to us through his word and we speak to him through prayer and praise. Neuburg and Sankt Joachimsthal have raised such rooms slightly earlier. This is the one that becomes the model.
suggested_refs: The Schlosskapelle at Hartenfels Castle, Torgau, dedicated by Luther 5 October 1544
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: The Preservation of the Church

stops.name: Halle, four days held by the river
stops.date_confidence: attested to late January 1546; the exact day of the Halle sermon is not fixed
stops.campa: On the way to Eisleben to arbitrate between the counts of Mansfeld, who have been quarrelling over mining rights and jurisdiction for years, the party is stopped four days at Halle by the flooded Saale. He preaches in the market church, where Justus Jonas is now pastor, and waits for the water to fall. He is sixty-two, dropsical, with angina and stones, travelling in a Thuringian winter to settle an argument about copper among the men who employed his father. He crosses at the end of January in a small boat, in the wind, and calls it the devil's work.
suggested_refs: The Marktkirche Unser Lieben Frauen at Halle, where Justus Jonas served as pastor
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: The Preservation of the Church

stops.name: Eisleben, the last night in the town of his birth
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the building is a reconstruction, see campa
stops.campa: The arbitration succeeds on the sixteenth. Two nights later, in the town where he was born, he wakes about one in the morning with pain across his chest, says the psalm in Latin, into thy hands I commend my spirit, thou hast redeemed me, God of truth, and answers Jonas clearly when asked whether he will stand by the doctrine he has taught. He is dead before three. Which house it happened in is disputed. The museum building on the Andreaskirchplatz has been called the death house only since the seventeenth century; recent research puts the death at Markt 56, in a building since demolished.
suggested_refs: Luthers Sterbehaus, Andreaskirchplatz 7, Eisleben, bought by Prussia for a memorial in 1863
sources: contemporary account by Justus Jonas, present at the deathbed

stops.name: Eisleben, the coffin at St. Andrew's
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The body is laid in a pewter coffin and carried to St. Andrew's, where he had preached four sermons in the last week of his life, the last of them broken off because he was too weak to finish it. Justus Jonas preaches the funeral sermon on the nineteenth and Michael Coelius preaches on the twentieth. Two days of watching follow, the town guilds and the counts' men standing by the coffin in turn. Then the Elector's order arrives from Wittenberg: the body is not to remain in Eisleben. Fifty horsemen take it out of the gate on the road north.
suggested_refs: St. Andreas, Eisleben, with the pulpit from which Luther preached his last sermons
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther: The Preservation of the Church

stops.name: Wittenberg, the grave beneath the pulpit
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The cortege comes through Halle and Bitterfeld with bells rung in every place it passes and reaches Wittenberg on the twenty-second. He is buried in the Castle Church, in the floor beside the pulpit, about two and a half metres down. Bugenhagen preaches and cannot finish for weeping. Melanchthon gives the Latin oration and says that a charioteer of Israel has fallen. Melanchthon is laid beside him in 1560, under a plate as plain as his. The door the theses may or may not have been nailed to is thirty paces away, and it burns in 1760.
suggested_refs: The Schlosskirche at Wittenberg, holding the graves of Luther and Melanchthon under bronze floor plates

stops.name: Torgau, the widow in the ditch
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Katharina runs the cloister as a farm and a boarding house for twenty-seven years, brews the beer, buys the land at Zulsdorf, and is left everything in a will that Saxon law does not permit a woman to receive. Plague and war drive her out of Wittenberg in 1552. The horses bolt on the road near Torgau, she is thrown into a ditch of cold water, and she dies there three months later at fifty-three. She is buried in the town church, fifty kilometres from her husband. In 1925 Ida Hoffmann will die in another Lutheran parsonage, in Parana, kept by a sister.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Katharina von Bora in the Marienkirche at Torgau, with its 1553 epitaph relief

stops.name: Wittenberg, the door cast in bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested; Gregorian, the calendar having changed in the interval
stops.campa: Fire takes the wooden doors when Imperial artillery shells the Prussian garrison in the town in 1760, so that the posting rests from then on entirely on testimony and not at all on wood. Ninety-eight years later Friedrich Wilhelm IV has bronze doors cast with the Latin theses on them, dedicated on the reformer's birthday: a thousand kilograms of Prussian state theology bolted where the paper may have hung. Nietzsche is born in a Lutheran parsonage fourteen years before the casting, Schelling has already sat under this doctrine at the Tuebingen Stift, and Max Mueller is shelving Luther at Oxford as the metal cools.
suggested_refs: The Thesentuer of 1858 at the Schlosskirche, Wittenberg, dedicated on the 375th anniversary of Luther's birth
